feature.title: Where to see his work
feature.lead: Almost everything Michelangelo made is still where people can visit it, in Florence, Rome and a few other cities. Here is where each great work is today.

items.label: David
items.text: Carved from a tall block that other sculptors had started and left about 25 years before. It stood outside the Palazzo Vecchio from 1504 and was moved indoors to the Accademia in 1873; a copy now stands in the square.

items.label: Pietà
items.text: Mary holding the body of Christ, made for a French cardinal when Michelangelo was in his early twenties. It is the only work he signed, across Mary's sash. It is in the first chapel on the north side after the entrance, behind protective glass.

items.label: Sistine Chapel ceiling
items.text: Scenes from Genesis with prophets, sibyls and over 300 figures, on a vault about 20 metres above the floor. He signed the contract on 8 May 1508 and it was revealed on 31 October 1512.

items.label: The Last Judgment
items.text: A huge fresco on the altar wall of the same chapel, painted in his sixties for Pope Paul III. Draperies were later painted over many figures after church critics objected.

items.label: Moses
items.text: The seated Moses at the centre of the tomb of Pope Julius II, a project that was cut down many times.

items.label: Medici Chapel (New Sacristy)
items.text: A chapel he designed as building and sculpture together, with the tombs of two Medici dukes and the figures of Night, Day, Dusk and Dawn. He left it unfinished when he moved to Rome in 1534.

items.label: Laurentian Library
items.text: A library for the Medici books, with a famous entrance hall and staircase. Others finished it from his plans, and it opened to scholars in 1571.

items.label: St Peter's dome
items.text: He became chief architect of St Peter's in his seventies and redesigned the great dome. The drum was complete when he died, and Giacomo della Porta and Domenico Fontana finished the dome in 1590.

items.label: Madonna of the Stairs and Battle of the Centaurs
items.text: Two marble reliefs carved in his teens in the Medici household, his earliest surviving sculptures. The family house that holds them is now a museum with about 200 of his drawings.

items.label: Bacchus
items.text: His first large statue in Rome, a tipsy god of wine. The cardinal who ordered it turned it down, and a banker bought it instead.

items.label: Madonna of Bruges
items.text: The first of his sculptures to leave Italy in his lifetime. Taken to Germany in 1944, it was found a year later in an Austrian salt mine and brought back.

items.label: Doni Tondo
items.text: A round painting of the Holy Family for Agnolo Doni, probably to mark his marriage or the birth of his daughter. It is the only finished panel painting of his mature years to survive.

items.label: Dying Slave
items.text: Made for the tomb of Julius II but never used there. He gave it to a friend who had cared for him during illness.

items.label: Piazza del Campidoglio
items.text: He redesigned the ancient hill as a square around the bronze horseman of Marcus Aurelius. Little was built in his lifetime, but it was finished to his design.

items.label: Florentine Pietà
items.text: Carved in old age, probably for his own tomb. The hooded figure is thought to be his self-portrait. Frustrated, he broke parts of it in 1555, and a pupil repaired some of them.

items.label: Rondanini Pietà
items.text: His last sculpture, still unfinished. He worked on it six days before he died. It has its own museum in the castle since 2015.

timeline.title: Born in Caprese
timeline.text: Michelangelo was born in the small town of Caprese, near Arezzo, where his father Lodovico was serving as a local official. The family was Florentine and had once been small-scale bankers.

timeline.title: Raised among stonecutters
timeline.text: His mother Francesca died when he was six. For a time he lived with a nurse and her stonecutter husband in Settignano, a quarry village. He later joked that he had taken in hammer and chisel with his nurse's milk.

timeline.title: Apprentice painter
timeline.text: At about 13 he was apprenticed to the painter Domenico Ghirlandaio. The next year his father arranged for him to be paid, which was rare for a boy his age.

timeline.title: In the Medici garden
timeline.text: Lorenzo de' Medici asked for Ghirlandaio's best pupils to study among the ancient statues in his garden. Michelangelo carved a faun's head there; Lorenzo noticed him and took him into his own household.

timeline.title: First marble reliefs
timeline.text: In the Medici household he carved the Madonna of the Stairs and the Battle of the Centaurs, his earliest surviving sculptures, about 1491 to 1492.

timeline.title: Lorenzo dies
timeline.text: His patron Lorenzo de' Medici died, and Michelangelo left the Medici court. He carved on his own and studied anatomy to understand the human body.

timeline.title: Leaving Florence
timeline.text: As the Medici were driven out of Florence, he left for Venice and then Bologna, where he carved small figures for the shrine of St Dominic.

timeline.title: To Rome
timeline.text: He arrived in Rome at the invitation of Cardinal Raffaele Riario. In July he began a statue of Bacchus, which the cardinal later refused.

timeline.title: The Pietà
timeline.text: He finished the Pietà for a French cardinal. Hearing it credited to another sculptor, he carved his name on Mary's sash. It is the only work he ever signed.

timeline.title: The giant block
timeline.text: The cathedral works in Florence gave him a huge marble block that two earlier sculptors had begun and abandoned decades before. He began carving the David in September.

timeline.title: David unveiled
timeline.text: A committee of leading artists, including Leonardo da Vinci and Botticelli, chose to place the David at the entrance of the Palazzo Vecchio. It was unveiled there and became a symbol of the city.

timeline.title: A tomb for a pope
timeline.text: Pope Julius II called him to Rome to make a grand tomb with about forty statues. He spent months in the Carrara quarries choosing marble. The project was cut down many times in the years that followed.

timeline.title: Walking out
timeline.text: After quarrels with the pope over the tomb, he left Rome secretly for Florence. Later that year he made peace with Julius in Bologna and was set to cast a bronze statue of him, "not my trade", as he wrote.

timeline.title: The ceiling
timeline.text: He signed the contract to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling. He had little experience of fresco and tried to avoid the job. He changed the plan from twelve apostles to scenes from Genesis, and had a free-standing scaffold built instead of one hung from holes in the ceiling. He painted standing, not lying on his back.

timeline.title: The ceiling revealed
timeline.text: The finished ceiling was revealed, and the pope said Mass in the chapel the next day. Condivi says he did it all without help, but he did have assistants for tasks such as preparing plaster and grinding colours.

timeline.title: Moses
timeline.text: After Julius died, the tomb was reduced. Michelangelo carved the seated Moses, about 1513 to 1515, and figures of captives for it.

timeline.title: A façade cancelled
timeline.text: After three years of designs and quarry work for a marble façade for San Lorenzo, ordered by Pope Leo X, the project was cancelled. The façade was never built.

timeline.title: The Medici Chapel
timeline.text: He began the New Sacristy at San Lorenzo, designing the building and its sculpted tombs together. He worked on it until 1534.

timeline.title: A library for the Medici
timeline.text: Building began on the Laurentian Library, commissioned by Pope Clement VII. "Architecture is not my profession", he had written, but his entrance hall and staircase became famous.

timeline.title: Defending the city
timeline.text: During the siege of Florence he worked on the city's fortifications.

timeline.title: In hiding
timeline.text: When Florence fell, he was condemned to death. He hid for about two months and was then pardoned.

timeline.title: Rome for good
timeline.text: He left Florence for Rome and never returned. He spent his last thirty years there.

timeline.title: The Last Judgment
timeline.text: He began painting the Last Judgment on the Sistine altar wall for Pope Paul III. The same year he made his first designs for a new square on the Capitoline Hill.

timeline.title: A friendship in sonnets
timeline.text: He became close friends with the poet Vittoria Colonna; sources disagree whether they met in 1536 or 1538. They exchanged sonnets until her death in 1547.

timeline.title: The Judgment finished
timeline.text: He finished the Last Judgment. Some church leaders objected to its nude figures, and later painters added draperies to many of them.

timeline.title: Architect of St Peter's
timeline.text: In his seventies he became chief architect of the new St Peter's Basilica. He went back to a centralised plan and redesigned the great dome.

timeline.title: A living legend
timeline.text: Giorgio Vasari published his Lives of the artists, including a life of Michelangelo, who was still alive. In 1553 his pupil Ascanio Condivi published a second life, partly to correct Vasari, with the master's help.

timeline.title: Carving by candlelight
timeline.text: He was carving a Pietà probably meant for his own tomb, and in frustration broke parts of it in 1555. Vasari, who knew him, says that in old age he often carved at night in a cap of thick paper with a candle on top, and that the hammer kept him healthy.

timeline.title: His death
timeline.text: Michelangelo died in Rome at 88. Six days before, he had spent the whole day carving the Rondanini Pietà, which he left unfinished.

timeline.title: Home to Florence
timeline.text: As he had wished, his body was taken from Rome to Florence. Duke Cosimo I gave him a state funeral, and Vasari designed his tomb in Santa Croce.

timeline.title: The dome is closed
timeline.text: Giacomo della Porta and Domenico Fontana completed the dome of St Peter's, building on the drum Michelangelo had finished.

works.title: Madonna of the Stairs
works.text: A shallow marble relief carved in his mid-teens, showing his study of Donatello. Casa Buonarroti, Florence.

works.title: Battle of the Centaurs
works.text: A crowded relief of struggling figures, made for Lorenzo de' Medici. Casa Buonarroti, Florence.

works.title: Bacchus
works.text: His first large statue, refused by the cardinal who ordered it. Bargello, Florence.

works.title: Pietà
works.text: Mary with the dead Christ, his only signed work. St Peter's Basilica.

works.title: David
works.text: A 5.17-metre marble figure carved from an abandoned block, 1501-1504. Galleria dell'Accademia, Florence.

works.title: Madonna of Bruges
works.text: Mary and the child Jesus, bought by the Mouscron brothers of Bruges. Church of Our Lady, Bruges.

works.title: Doni Tondo
works.text: A round Holy Family panel, his only surviving finished panel painting from his mature years. Uffizi, Florence.

works.title: Sistine Chapel ceiling
works.text: Frescoes of Genesis, prophets and sibyls painted 1508-1512. Vatican Museums.

works.title: Moses
works.text: The seated prophet at the heart of the tomb of Julius II. San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome.

works.title: Dying Slave
works.text: A captive figure made for the Julius tomb and later given to a friend. Louvre, Paris.

works.title: New Sacristy (Medici Chapel)
works.text: Chapel, tombs and figures of Night, Day, Dusk and Dawn, 1520-1534. San Lorenzo, Florence.

works.title: Laurentian Library
works.text: The Medici library with its sculptural staircase hall, finished by others to his designs. Florence.

works.title: Piazza del Campidoglio
works.text: A new square on Rome's Capitoline Hill around the statue of Marcus Aurelius, completed after his death to his design.

works.title: The Last Judgment
works.text: The great altar-wall fresco of the Sistine Chapel, 1536-1541. Vatican Museums.

works.title: Dome of St Peter's
works.text: His redesign of the dome, finished in 1590 after his death. St Peter's Basilica, Vatican City.

works.title: Florentine Pietà
works.text: A late group meant for his own tomb, with a hooded figure thought to be his self-portrait. Museo dell'Opera del Duomo, Florence.

works.title: Rondanini Pietà
works.text: His last, unfinished sculpture. Castello Sforzesco, Milan.

works.title: Sonnets and madrigals
works.text: Many poems written across his life, about art, love, faith and old age, many to Tommaso dei Cavalieri and Vittoria Colonna.
